strengths: Addresses an important and ambitious problem: autonomous development and optimization of scientific computational methods using LLM agents, with potential impact in AI-for-science and computational biology.

Proposes a coherent agentic system with several concrete components: a domain-knowledge tree, category-level instruction sampling with Bayesian-style updates, diversity-promoting top-solution selection, and diagnostic feedback for model improvement.

Provides strong empirical coverage across 11 diverse tasks: 6 single-cell analysis benchmarks and 5 scientific deep-learning benchmarks, with comparisons against expert methods, MLE agents, and scientific agents.

Ablation studies and LLM-backbone analyses are included, showing that removing domain knowledge, category structure, Bayesian sampling, or diagnostics generally degrades performance, and that lower-cost LLMs can remain competitive.

Case studies on scDRS and pgBoost demonstrate practical utility: improvements over state-of-the-art genetics methods, concise/interpretable optimized functions, and biologically plausible discoveries such as disease-associated T cell subtypes and variant-gene links.

The paper includes detailed appendix material, example prompts, task setup, and optimization templates, which improves transparency and supports reproducibility if the code and data are properly released.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than decisive: the core ingredients—LLM-driven code optimization, tree search/instruction categories, Bayesian/bandit-style sampling, and diagnostic feedback—are individually familiar; the contribution is mainly their combination and application to scientific method development.

Evaluation fairness is not fully convincing: TusoAI and AIDE are run for 8 hours, while Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent are constrained by web interfaces, file-size limits, and 1-hour runtimes, so scientific-agent comparisons are not apples-to-apples. Expert baselines are also partly selected from existing benchmarks with efficiency filters.

Main claims are sometimes overstated. TusoAI does not consistently beat all baselines on the deep-learning tasks, and average performance is only marginally better than DARTS/expert in some settings; "outperforms state-of-the-art expert methods" is stronger than the evidence supports.

The genetics case-study claims of "novel biology" are based on computational predictions without experimental validation. Novel variant-gene links and disease–T cell associations should be framed as hypotheses requiring follow-up, not established biology.

Reproducibility has gaps: the manuscript says the code is publicly available but provides no actual URL in the PDF; the reference list contains duplicated and malformed entries, and some baseline/evaluation details are relegated to appendices.

Methodological details could be better justified: the Bayesian category update only increases probabilities after successful optimizations and lacks an explicit penalty/decay for repeatedly poor categories; the diagnostic optimization path is only 20% by default and shows mixed ablation gains.

Statistical rigor is limited: some single-cell claims rely on 3 random seeds with reported CIs under 0.01, deep-learning CIs are provided but significance tests across tasks are absent, and multiple comparisons across many benchmarks/case studies are not adjusted.
The heuristic of choosing the shortest solution within 0.1% of the cluster best may bias toward smaller code and could remove genuinely better but more complex methods; its effect is not ablated.

Clarity and consistency issues remain: the abstract/section numbers for pgBoost improvements are expressed differently (e.g., 10.5% vs. 13.8%/7.2%), and the paper's broad scope makes it difficult to verify all claims from the main text alone.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: automating development and optimization of computational methods for scientific domains.
Presents a complete system design with domain knowledge integration, iterative optimization, feedback, and diagnostic prompting.
Evaluates on a relatively broad set of 11 tasks (6 single-cell, 5 scientific deep-learning) and includes ablations over several components and LLM backbones.
Includes two genetics case studies demonstrating potential practical utility and low-cost optimization of existing methods (scDRS, pgBoost).
Provides algorithm pseudocode, prompt templates, and a code template, which help clarify the intended workflow.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core components (knowledge retrieval, category sampling, feedback, diagnostic prompting, tree-search-like optimization) are combinations of existing ideas in LLM agents, AutoML, and Bayesian optimization, with no strong theoretical or algorithmic advance. The 'Bayesian updates' are heuristic multiplicative updates, not a principled Bayesian method, and the 'knowledge tree' is essentially a two-level category-instruction list.

Baseline comparisons are not convincing or fair. Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent are run through web interfaces with limited runtimes and iteration counts, while TusoAI is run for 8 hours in a controlled environment. Only AIDE is included among MLE agents, despite related work mentioning MLE-STAR, R&D-Agent, DS-Agent, and AutoML-Agent. No comparison is made to several relevant concurrent or recent method-development agents.

Deep-learning benchmark results do not support the claim of consistently outperforming baselines. In Table 2, TusoAI has average 0.70 while DARTS has average 0.71, and the margin over the expert average is only 0.01. TusoAI is worse than expert on ECG and NinaPro, and the reported 'average rank' highlights selective ranking rather than overall performance.

Case studies overclaim 'novel biology'. The scDRS and pgBoost comparisons are mainly against the original methods, not against other state-of-the-art alternatives for the same problems. The newly reported disease-cell and variant-gene links are not experimentally validated and are better framed as hypotheses, not established discoveries.

There are inconsistent numbers across the paper: the abstract claims a 10.5% enrichment improvement for pgBoost, while Section 5 reports 13.8% for eQTL and 7.2% for ABC. Such inconsistencies weaken confidence in the reported gains.

Statistical reliability is questionable. The paper claims 95% CIs under 0.01 for single-cell tasks and thus omits them, but Appendix Figure 5 shows large variation across three TusoAI optimization replicates for tasks such as Decomposition and Visual. Ablation differences also lack significance tests, and some ablations show that removing components can improve individual tasks, contradicting the claimed importance of diagnosis and categories.

The method restricts the search space to a single function within a provided template for many experiments. This undermines the broad claim of autonomously developing computational methods from scratch, since data loading, evaluation, and overall pipeline structure are fixed.

Several design choices are arbitrary or insufficiently justified: initializing earlier pipeline categories with higher probability, using a 1.1 multiplicative update, choosing the shortest solution within 0.1% of the best, and imposing strict 10-minute implementation limits. These choices may strongly affect results and are not ablated thoroughly.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code URL is missing, baseline web-agent runs are not fully reproducible, and important implementation details (prompts, budget allocation, failure handling, variance across runs) are only partially specified.

Writing and references contain serious defects. Several references are corrupted or duplicated, e.g., AIDE is cited as 'Biomechanical ai agent' and multiple entries repeat the same incorrect reference. Algorithm 1 also has formatting and consistency issues. This harms clarity and credibility.

The paper does not sufficiently isolate why TusoAI works. The diversity analysis shows higher code diversity than AIDE, but diversity alone does not imply better search; no controlled study links diversity, diagnostic feedback, and Bayesian category sampling to final performance with statistical rigor.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: automating development and optimization of computational methods for scientific domains, bridging scientific analysis agents and general ML engineering agents.
Presents a well-engineered agentic framework combining a domain knowledge tree, hierarchical planning with category-level sampling, diagnostic feedback, and iterative solution refinement.

Provides broad empirical evaluation on 6 single-cell OpenProblems tasks and 5 NASBench-360 scientific deep learning tasks, with ablations, LLM backbone analysis, diversity measurements, and optimization trajectories.
Achieves strong single-cell benchmark results: average rank 1.2 versus 3.0 for the second-best method and an average 16% improvement, with substantial gains on denoising, SVG, and decomposition.

Includes two compelling genetics case studies: TusoAI improves scDRS with over 40% higher power in causal simulations and improves pgBoost with 13.8% higher eQTL enrichment plus newly proposed variant-gene links.
Demonstrates cost-efficiency: default GPT-4o-mini remains competitive with much more expensive reasoning models, enabling low-cost optimization runs.
Reproducibility is generally good: code is public, prompts and instruction-generation templates are provided, and benchmark setup details are documented in appendices.
The code diversity and optimization trajectory analyses provide useful insight into why the method explores more broadly than AIDE.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core ingredients—LLM agents, tree search, retrieval, bandit-style sampling, and feedback—are largely combinations of existing ideas; the knowledge tree and Bayesian update are heuristic rather than deeply novel.

Some claims are overstated. The paper states TusoAI consistently outperforms expert methods across benchmarks, but on deep learning tasks DARTS has a higher average (0.71 vs. 0.70) and TusoAI is not best on several tasks such as Spherical, NinaPro, ECG, and DeepSEA.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair. Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent are run through web interfaces with 1-hour limits and far fewer iterations, while TusoAI is given 8 hours; AIDE also faced timeout issues. Deep learning baselines are precomputed and may not match TusoAI's compute budget.

The ablation study does not strongly support the diagnostic component: removing diagnosis gives average 0.64 vs. default 0.66 with the same average rank, and performance improves on some tasks while dropping on others. No confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported for ablations.

The category update is described as Bayesian but is only a multiplicative increase on success with renormalization; there is no clear probabilistic posterior over categories, no penalty or decay for failures, and limited analysis of this component.

Evaluation coverage is limited in places: single-cell results use only 3 seeds, some deep learning tasks are excluded, and several baseline numbers are taken from prior work rather than rerun under controlled settings.

The case studies optimize only a single function within existing SOTA methods, and the new biological findings are plausible but not experimentally validated; simulation-based optimization may also overfit to the chosen effect-size regime.

Some presentation and framing issues remain: the abstract and conclusions overstate generality on deep learning tasks, while the empirical tables show mixed results and reliance on average-rank metrics that can obscure per-task losses.

strengths: Tackles an important and timely problem: automating scientific method development rather than only composing existing tools or pipelines.
Proposes a concrete agentic system that integrates literature-derived structured knowledge, iterative optimization, diagnostics, feedback, and category-level sampling.
Provides extensive empirical evaluation across 6 single-cell tasks and 5 scientific deep learning tasks, with comparisons to MLE agents, scientific agents, expert methods, and NAS baselines.
Includes useful ablations on core components and LLM backbones, plus analyses of code diversity, runtime, cost, and optimization trajectories.

Single-cell results are strong (average rank 1.2), and the two genetics case studies are compelling: TusoAI improves scDRS and pgBoost and reports new trait-cell-type associations and variant-gene links with biological plausibility.
Appendices provide substantial implementation detail, prompts, task setups, and additional analyses, which helps reproducibility despite reliance on closed LLMs.
weaknesses: Novelty is mainly system-level integration; the knowledge tree, Bayesian-style category updates, feedback, and diagnostic optimization are combinations of existing LLM-agent, search, and AutoML ideas, and the 1.1 multiplicative update is heuristic rather than principled Bayesian inference.

Deep learning results are not consistently superior: TusoAI's average (0.70) is below DARTS (0.71), and it loses on several tasks such as Spherical, NinaPro, and ECG, so claims of consistent or broadly superior performance are overstated.

Baseline fairness is questionable: AIDE's timeout was left at 1 hour due to crashes, Biomni/ChatGPT-Agent were substituted by best-of-10 LLM outputs on deep learning tasks, and expert methods were selected partly by runtime constraints.

The case studies optimize only a single function within a large codebase and rely on existing evaluation functions, limiting generality and raising the risk of overfitting to the validation objective over long optimization runs.

Reproducibility and clarity are partially limited by many heuristic hyperparameters, nondeterministic closed-source LLM calls, and an optimization process that depends heavily on prompt engineering and implementation details.
No substantial discussion of ethical or dual-use implications for automated genetics method discovery, despite applications involving disease-associated variants and human genetic data.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: automating the development and optimization of scientific computational methods using LLM agents.
Combines domain literature, structured instruction categories, a knowledge-tree representation, iterative code optimization, and diagnostic feedback into a single agentic framework.
Provides a broad empirical evaluation across 11 tasks, including 6 single-cell analysis benchmarks and 5 scientific deep learning benchmarks, plus two genetics case studies.

The case studies on scDRS and pgBoost show concrete improvements over strong expert methods and generate biologically plausible discoveries, such as novel T-cell disease associations and a GCK variant-gene link.
Includes a substantial appendix with prompt templates, task setups, additional analyses, and an open-source code statement.
Conducts ablation studies and LLM-backbone comparisons, attempting to isolate the contribution of domain knowledge, Bayesian sampling, diagnosis, and different base models.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the system largely combines existing ideas such as LLM-driven code search, instruction sampling, tree search, feedback, and self-diagnosis. The claimed 'Bayesian update' is a heuristic multiplicative change (π_c ← 1.1π_c), not Bayesian inference.

Baseline comparisons are not convincingly fair. Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent are run through web interfaces with file-size/runtime constraints, AIDE is run with default timeouts after crashes, and deep-learning 'agentic' baselines are substituted with best-of-10 static LLM outputs rather than comparable iterative agents.
AIDE is allowed to edit the evaluation function in the decomposition task, yet its resulting score is still reported in Table 1, undermining the validity of that comparison.

The central claim that TusoAI 'outperforms state-of-the-art expert methods, MLE agents, and scientific AI agents across diverse tasks' is overstated. TusoAI is not best on average for the deep-learning tasks (DARTS has higher average performance), and it is worse than ChatGPT-Agent on decomposition, Expert on ECG, and Claude-4-Sonnet on DeepSEA.

Ablation results are inconsistent: removing diagnosis improves performance on some tasks (e.g., decomposition and ECG), and the main ablation table lacks statistical tests and is limited to five tasks.

Task selection and metric choices may be cherry-picked: several benchmark tasks are excluded for various reasons, metrics are modified or normalized, and expert baselines are chosen partly by runtime efficiency rather than exhaustively representing SOTA.

Case-study validation is computational rather than experimental, so the 'new biology' claims remain hypotheses. The concurrent work by Aygün et al. is not directly compared despite addressing a similar problem.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript's code URL is missing, exact LLM versions/API endpoints and compute budgets are not fully specified, and some cost/time claims (e.g., 167 variations in 24 hours at $0.37) are not sufficiently supported.

Acknowledged limitations are significant: the method requires a predefined evaluator, operates best on a single function within a large codebase, does not invent new evaluation procedures, and relies on heuristic components without theoretical guarantees.

strengths: Introduces TusoAI, a clear and practically relevant agentic system for optimizing scientific computational methods, with an explicit focus on domain-specific method development rather than only pipeline execution or general ML engineering.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 11 scientific tasks, including 6 single-cell analysis benchmarks and 5 scientific deep learning benchmarks, with comparisons to expert methods, MLE agents, scientific AI agents, and NAS baselines.

Strong benchmark performance: TusoAI achieves the best average rank on both benchmark suites and improves over expert baselines on average, with concrete examples of non-trivial discovered methods such as NMF with dropout/Poisson modeling for denoising.
Well-structured ablation studies that isolate the effects of knowledge categories, Bayesian sampling, diagnosis, and domain knowledge, showing that domain knowledge has the largest impact.

Two compelling genetics case studies (scDRS and pgBoost) demonstrate real-world applicability, significant quantitative improvements, and biologically plausible new discoveries at low computational cost.

Good reproducibility signals: code is publicly available, prompt templates and implementation details are provided in appendices, and the method is evaluated with multiple LLM backbones and cost/runtime analyses.
The paper is generally well written and positions the work clearly relative to scientific AI agents, MLE agents, and classical AutoML/NAS approaches.
weaknesses: The claimed “Bayesian” update is a heuristic multiplicative reweighting (e.g., π_c ← 1.1π_c) rather than a principled probabilistic model; the paper should avoid overstating this as Bayesian inference.

The core novelty is somewhat incremental: knowledge trees, draft-then-refine prompting, LLM-based code optimization, and bandit-like category sampling are existing ideas combined into a useful system, but the paper does not provide new theoretical insight or a fundamentally new algorithm.

Some comparisons are not fully convincing: Biomni and ChatGPT-Agent are used through web interfaces with iteration/time constraints, and for deep learning tasks the LLM baselines are one-shot rather than iterative agents, which may disadvantage them relative to TusoAI.

The abstract/introduction claim of “consistently outperforming” is stronger than the evidence: TusoAI does not win every task (e.g., ECG, DeepSEA, NinaPro), and on the deep learning benchmark its average score (0.70) is slightly below DARTS (0.71), even though its average rank is better.
The “No diagnosis” ablation is not clearly worse than the default setting on all tasks and has the same average rank, weakening the case for the diagnostic-based optimization component.

TusoAI operates on a single function and requires an evaluation function; extending to large, multi-file scientific codebases or missing/imperfect evaluators is not solved and remains a significant practical limitation for autonomous scientific discovery.

The new biological findings are validated computationally against known biology and enrichment benchmarks, but not experimentally, so the “new biology” claim should be framed more cautiously as hypothesis generation.
